scenes.tts: A bulk RNA reading rises. Did any cell turn the gene up? Chapter one ended on a lining whose mix of cells had changed. Gold clones spread, though on average their cells divided no faster. Now grind that lining up and measure one RNA.
scenes.visual: Open on chapter 1's last picture: the top-down honeycomb of about 200 hexagons, BLUE with irregular GOLD patches covering a large share, faint shimmer, label top left 'mouse oesophagus' and 'schematic' in the corner. A plain outlined test tube and resting gauge labelled 'bulk reading' sit on the right. On the opening question, the line 'Did any cell turn it up?' appears across the top in white. On 'Chapter one ended', the question shrinks but remains visible. On 'grind that lining up', the honeycomb is scooped into the tube; the hexagons tumble in and blur into one even khaki-coloured liquid.
scenes.narration: A bulk RNA reading rises. Did any cell turn the gene up? Chapter one ended on a lining whose mix of cells had changed. Gold clones spread, though on average their cells divided no faster. Now grind that lining up and measure one RNA.

scenes.visual: Title 'The Mix Moves the Average' fades in over the top for 2 s; the liquid in the tube swirls slowly. The question text fades out under it.

scenes.tts: Suppose, with made-up numbers, each gold cell holds twenty copies of one RNA. Each blue cell holds ten. Suppose our bulk assay reports copies per average cell.
scenes.caption: Suppose, with made-up numbers, each gold cell holds 20 copies of one RNA. Each blue cell holds 10. Suppose our bulk assay reports copies per average cell.
scenes.visual: THE WORLD for this chapter: left two-thirds, a tray of exactly 10 round cells in two rows (enlarged versions of chapter 1's basal cells), each with a small bar above it showing its RNA level; right third, the tube and the 'bulk reading' gauge. Corner label 'made-up numbers'. On 'each gold cell', gold cells' bars rise to a mark labelled '20'; on 'each blue cell', blue bars rise to '10'. On 'bulk assay', all ten bars pour as streams into the tube, and the gauge needle swings to the average. Label under the gauge: 'copies per average cell'. Bars never change height while the cells sit in the tray.
scenes.narration: Suppose, with made-up numbers, each gold cell holds 20 copies of one RNA. Each blue cell holds 10. Suppose our bulk assay reports copies per average cell.

scenes.tts: Early on, gold cells are two in ten. Two tenths of twenty, plus eight tenths of ten, gives twelve copies per average cell.
scenes.caption: Early on, gold cells are 2 in 10. Two tenths of 20, plus eight tenths of 10, gives 12 copies per average cell.
scenes.visual: The tray shows 2 GOLD and 8 BLUE cells, with 'early' above it. A computed sum builds in the right panel term by term as spoken: '0.2 × 20 = 4', '0.8 × 10 = 8', then '= 12 per cell'. The gauge needle settles exactly on 12 on a scale marked 0 to 20; a thin tick stays at 12 as a marker for later.
scenes.narration: Early on, gold cells are 2 in 10. Two tenths of 20, plus eight tenths of 10, gives 12 copies per average cell.

scenes.tts: Later, the clones have spread, and gold cells are six in ten. No single cell changes how much RNA it holds. Does the bulk reading go up, go down, or stay the same?
scenes.caption: Later, the clones have spread, and gold cells are 6 in 10. No single cell changes how much RNA it holds. Does the bulk reading go up, go down, or stay the same?
scenes.visual: Label above the tray morphs from 'early' to 'later'. One at a time, four BLUE cells in the tray turn GOLD (soft flash each) until there are 6 GOLD and 4 BLUE; each cell's bar keeps exactly its colour's height (gold 20, blue 10), and the label 'no cell changes its level' appears under the tray. The gauge needle is hidden behind a small grey cover. On 'Does the bulk reading', the question card appears in the right panel in white: 'Up, down or the same?'.
scenes.narration: Later, the clones have spread, and gold cells are 6 in 10. No single cell changes how much RNA it holds. Does the bulk reading go up, go down, or stay the same?

scenes.visual: Hold the question card. Near-silence. Only slow ambient motion: the bars above the cells shimmer gently at fixed heights and the liquid in the tube swirls. The gauge stays covered.

scenes.tts: It goes up. Six tenths of twenty, plus four tenths of ten, gives sixteen. The reading rose by a third, yet no cell turned its gene up. Only the mix changed.
scenes.caption: It goes up. Six tenths of 20, plus four tenths of 10, gives 16. The reading rose by a third, yet no cell turned its gene up. Only the mix changed.
scenes.visual: The question card slides away. The computed sum builds in the right panel term by term: '0.6 × 20 = 12', '0.4 × 10 = 4', '= 16 per cell'. The cover lifts and the needle swings from the old tick at 12 to 16; a bracket between the two marks reads 'up by a third'. On 'no cell turned its gene up', every bar in the tray pulses once at its unchanged height. On 'Only the mix changed', the gold cells in the tray pulse together.
scenes.narration: It goes up. Six tenths of 20, plus four tenths of 10, gives 16. The reading rose by a third, yet no cell turned its gene up. Only the mix changed.

scenes.tts: That is the idea of this lesson. A tissue can change because which cells are there changes, not only because its cells behave differently. On its own, one average cannot tell those apart.
scenes.visual: The tray and tube shrink to the left. In the right panel, two short lines appear side by side, each with a tiny icon: 'which cells are there' (tray with more gold cells, bars unchanged) and 'how cells behave' (same tray, every bar taller). Both icons feed an arrow into one identical gauge reading 16. On 'cannot tell those apart', the two arrows pulse together into the single gauge and a white '?' appears over it.
scenes.narration: That is the idea of this lesson. A tissue can change because which cells are there changes, not only because its cells behave differently. On its own, one average cannot tell those apart.

scenes.tts: To estimate the mix, measure sampled cells one at a time. Single-cell RNA sequencing usually starts by separating tissue into single cells, often with enzymes. Each captured RNA is copied into DNA carrying a short barcode for its cell.
scenes.visual: Back to the full tray, now holding about 30 cells: BLUE and GREEN keratinocytes at different points in differentiation, GOLD cells with the toy RNA profile, plus a few small PURPLE T cells. Do not label the identities yet. On 'separating tissue', the cells drift apart from one another into single file. On 'copied into DNA', each cell releases a few labelled 'captured RNA' chips that transform into plain 'DNA copy' chips; a short coloured stripe, different for each cell, appears on every DNA copy from that cell. Label the stripe 'cell barcode'. Use chips only, not molecular structures. Corner label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: To estimate the mix, measure sampled cells one at a time. Single-cell RNA sequencing usually starts by separating tissue into single cells, often with enzymes. Each captured RNA is copied into DNA carrying a short barcode for its cell.

scenes.tts: Sequencing produces a count for each gene in each sampled cell. The result is a table, with one row per gene and one column per sampled cell. Software groups cells with similar expression profiles into clusters.
scenes.visual: The barcoded DNA-copy chips stream to the right and sort themselves by stripe into columns, building a grid: rows labelled 'genes', columns labelled 'sampled cells', each square shaded by its count (darker = more). Title above the grid: 'count matrix'. On 'groups cells', the columns lift off the grid as dots and drift onto a plain 2D field, where they gather into four loose clouds coloured by the cells they came from (blue, green, gold, purple). Label 'clusters'. Corner label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Sequencing produces a count for each gene in each sampled cell. The result is a table, with one row per gene and one column per sampled cell. Software groups cells with similar expression profiles into clusters.

scenes.tts: Clusters are annotated by comparing their genes with known profiles. Now the shift can be estimated. The gold-profile group contains more sampled cells, while its within-group RNA level stays fixed.
scenes.visual: Name tags appear beside three clouds one at a time: 'progenitor', 'differentiating' and 'T cell'. The gold cloud gets the deliberately provisional label 'gold-profile group?' rather than 'clone': RNA profiles alone do not establish clonal ancestry. On 'shift can be estimated', the label 'early sample' appears and the gold cloud is small; it morphs to 'later sample' and the gold cloud fills in with more dots while the other clouds thin slightly. A small bar inside each cloud, its RNA level for the made-up gene, stays at the same height throughout; keep the established gold and blue values at 20 and 10, and leave the other bars unnumbered. Corner labels 'sampled cells' and 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Clusters are annotated by comparing their genes with known profiles. Now the shift can be estimated. The gold-profile group contains more sampled cells, while its within-group RNA level stays fixed.

scenes.tts: But what does a cluster represent? It might mark a cell type, a relatively stable identity such as a keratinocyte or T cell. It might instead mark a state within one type, such as dividing or differentiating. This distinction depends on the question.
scenes.visual: Fade the name tags. A large white bracket wraps the blue and green clouds together, labelled 'one type: keratinocyte'; the purple cloud gets 'one type: T cell'. On 'state within one type', a few dots in the blue cloud get small spinning clock faces (chapter 1's division clocks) and slide to one edge of the cloud, and the label 'state: dividing' appears beside them. The blue and green groups get the qualified label 'differentiation states here'. Leave the gold cloud's question mark in place. Corner label 'working definitions'.
scenes.narration: But what does a cluster represent? It might mark a cell type, a relatively stable identity such as a keratinocyte or T cell. It might instead mark a state within one type, such as dividing or differentiating. This distinction depends on the question.

scenes.tts: Or it might reflect the method. Breaking up tissue can stress cells before capture. Cells from samples processed separately can split by batch. A clustering resolution setting can split or merge groups.
scenes.visual: Three small cartoon events happen on the cluster field, one per sentence, each with a label of at most 4 words: 'dissociation stress' (some dots flicker red and drift into a new small cloud of their own); 'batch effect' (the purple cloud splits into two halves that differ only in a tiny sample tag, 'sample 1' and 'sample 2'); 'resolution' (a slider labelled 'resolution' slides right and the blue cloud cracks into several fragments, then back left and the fragments merge). Corner label 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Or it might reflect the method. Breaking up tissue can stress cells before capture. Cells from samples processed separately can split by batch. A clustering resolution setting can split or merge groups.

scenes.tts: A cluster is an observation; what it represents is a hypothesis. A snapshot cannot reveal ancestry or future fate. Lineage tracing tests those. Perturbation tests cause, and protein can check an annotation.
scenes.visual: All clouds gain a small white '?' tag. Three labelled tiles build in the right panel, one per test: 'lineage' (a gold mark passing from a cell to its daughters, the chapter 1 clone outline), 'perturbation' (a cell with one part crossed out), 'protein' (a labelled surface-marker chip beside a matching detection tag). Use icons and chips only, not molecular structures. The clouds keep a slow breathing motion.
scenes.narration: A cluster is an observation; what it represents is a hypothesis. A snapshot cannot reveal ancestry or future fate. Lineage tracing tests those. Perturbation tests cause, and protein can check an annotation.

scenes.tts: Back in the lining, gold cells became common, so the average moved. No cell made more RNA. Change the mix; the average moves without within-cell change.
scenes.visual: The cluster field folds back into the top-down honeycomb from the hook, gold patches spread among the blue. The 'bulk reading' gauge beside it rests at 16 with the old tick at 12. On 'No cell made more RNA', every hexagon's tiny bar pulses at its unchanged height. On the final sentence, the patches and gauge pulse in turn.
scenes.narration: Back in the lining, gold cells became common, so the average moved. No cell made more RNA. Change the mix; the average moves without within-cell change.

scenes.visual: End card: the line below in white on the dark ground, with the small gauge beside it.
scenes.line: Change the mix; the average moves without within-cell change.
